title: The lived experience of adults and youths with physical disability and access to rehabilitation services: A scoping review and synthesis of qualitative evidence from Nepal
content:
by Winston Chin, Shermin Tan, Mark T. Carew, Thomas Shakespeare, Jane Wilbur

Persons with disability experience poorer health, access to education and employment, and living standards compared to persons without disability. Rehabilitation services can improve the functioning and social inclusion of persons with disability; however, access to rehabilitation in low- and middle-income countries is poor. Greater understanding is needed on how access to rehabilitation is influenced by lived experience and socio-cultural contexts. This scoping review synthesizes the literature on the lived experience of adults and youths with physical disability in Nepal and how it influences their access to rehabilitation, and identifies knowledge gaps. The protocol is registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF, doi https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/FWY7A). Five databases and other sources were searched until August 2025 for qualitative studies examining the lived experience of adults and youths with physical disability and/or their experience in accessing rehabilitation services in Nepal. All search results were screened for inclusion independently by two reviewers. Framework Synthesis was used as methodology for data extraction and synthesis, based on the One-Line Flower conceptual framework. Out of 1,995 screened results, 71 studies were included. Adults and youths with physical disability in Nepal experience numerous challenges and barriers at the personal, social and structural levels that significantly impact their physical, psycho-emotional and economic well-being, and social inclusion. However, they receive multi-faceted support from others, and exercise agency in the face of barriers. Although limited, evidence suggests that access to rehabilitation may be affected by economic challenges, attitudinal barriers, and poor accessibility and availability of services. Key limitations of the evidence base include a high proportion of unspecified physical disability types and a geographical skew towards urban areas. More research is needed into the factors that promote personal agency, changes in societal attitudes and norms, and access to rehabilitation, to support policies and interventions that improve the well-being of persons with disability.
